```{python}
import sys
import json
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

MLFIN_STYLE = {
    "figure.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "axes.facecolor": "#fcfcfb",
    "savefig.facecolor": "#fcfcfb",
    "font.family": ["Segoe UI", "Arial", "sans-serif"],
    "font.size": 12, "text.color": "#141413", "axes.edgecolor": "#c3c2b7",
    "axes.labelcolor": "#52514e", "axes.titlecolor": "#141413",
    "axes.titlesize": 13, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": "#e6e5df", "grid.linewidth": 0.8,
    "axes.axisbelow": True,
    "xtick.color": "#898781", "ytick.color": "#898781",
    "xtick.labelsize": 10.5, "ytick.labelsize": 10.5,
    "legend.frameon": False, "legend.fontsize": 10.5,
}
plt.rcParams.update(MLFIN_STYLE)

if not Path("data/power.csv").exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "Missing data/power.csv - run tools/build_session10_table.py from the repository root."
    )
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path("../tools").resolve()))
import deck10_data
import deck10_widgets as W

POWER = deck10_data.read("data")
DATA = deck10_data.build("data")
if DATA["lab"] is None:
    raise FileNotFoundError("Missing data/lab.json - run python tools/deck10_data.py session_10/data --lab")
MAP = json.loads(Path("data/map.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
HEAT = DATA["heat"]
STILL_DAY = HEAT["days"].index("2024-10-04")
TT_MARKS = {"the wind falls all day": "2024-12-10", "the wind rises all day": "2024-10-16",
            "a Monday": "2024-01-08"}

BLUE = "#1c5cab"
BLUE_LIGHT = "#86b6ef"
DEEP = "#0d366b"
AMBER = "#b8860b"
BRICK = "#b3402f"
GREY = "#c3c2b7"
INK = "#141413"
MUTED = "#52514e"


def hour_axis(ax):
    ax.set_xticks([0, 6, 12, 18, 23])
    ax.set_xticklabels(["00:00", "06:00", "12:00", "18:00", "23:00"])
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
```

# The question for 2024

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_a, _b = POWER.loc["2023-11-13"], POWER.loc["2023-11-14"]
_h, _pa, _pb = _a["hour"].to_numpy(), _a["price"].to_numpy(), _b["price"].to_numpy()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.6, 3.9))
ax.fill_between(_h, _pa, _pb, where=_pb > _pa, interpolate=True, color=BRICK, alpha=0.3, linewidth=0)
ax.fill_between(_h, _pa, _pb, where=_pb <= _pa, interpolate=True, color=BLUE, alpha=0.28, linewidth=0)
ax.plot(_h, _pa, color="#898781", linewidth=2.2)
ax.plot(_h, _pb, color=DEEP, linewidth=2.8)
ax.text(23.4, _pa[-1], "Today", color="#898781", va="center", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(23.4, _pb[-1], "Tomorrow", color=DEEP, va="center", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(2.5, (_pa[2] + _pb[2]) / 2, "lower tomorrow", color=BLUE, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(20.2, 775, "higher tomorrow", color=BRICK, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 26.4)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_bounds(0, 23)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1200)
ax.set_ylabel("kr per MWh")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.StrMethodFormatter("{x:,.0f}"))
hour_axis(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Will tomorrow's price at this hour be higher than today's? In this example the
answer is no until 14:00, and yes from 15:00.

On a spot-price contract a household pays each hour's price, plus tariffs and
taxes. For 170 kWh, the spot part cost 578 kroner in August 2022 and 93 in
August 2024.

Denmark is two price areas, joined to five neighbours by cable. The auction

already known. The forecast in the file comes out at 18:00 and stands in for a
bidder's own.

The offers are stacked from cheapest to most expensive, and the last one needed

# Reading the file

```{pyodide}
power = pd.read_csv("data/power.csv", parse_dates=["time"])
power = power.set_index("time")

print(power.shape)
power.head()
```

The table has 26,133 rows, one per hour from 2022 to 2024. With `time` as the
index, `.loc` picks out a day, a month or a year.


# The columns

<table class="vocab">
<tr><td>price</td><td>the day-ahead price in West Denmark, kroner per MWh</td><td><strong>wind</strong></td><td>the forecast of wind output, MW</td></tr>
<tr><td>date</td><td>the day, as text: 2024-10-04</td><td><strong>solar</strong></td><td>the forecast of solar output, MW</td></tr>
<tr><td>hour</td><td>the clock hour, 0 to 23</td><td><strong>time</strong></td><td>the index: the hour, Danish time</td></tr>
<tr><td>weekday</td><td>0 for Monday to 6 for Sunday</td><td><strong>weekend</strong></td><td>1 on a Saturday or a Sunday</td></tr>
</table>

Seven days with no published forecast are left out. On the day the clocks go
forward there are 23 hours, and on the day they go back the repeated hour is
averaged.


# A price per year

```{pyodide}
prices = power['price']

print(prices.groupby(power.index.year).mean())
print(prices.max())
```

The average hour cost 1,630 kroner in 2022 and 531 in 2024, a fall of two
thirds. The most expensive hour, at 17:00 on 12 December 2024, cost 6,982.


# Prices below zero

```{pyodide}
below = power['price'] < 0

print(below.groupby(power.index.year).sum())
print(prices.min())
```

The price was below zero in 360 hours of 2024, so buyers were paid to take the
power; the lowest, in July 2023, was 3,277 kroner below zero.

# The shape of a day

```{pyodide}
by_hour = power.groupby('hour')['price'].mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.4))
ax.plot(by_hour.index, by_hour.values)
ax.set_xlabel("hour of the day")
plt.show()
```

The average price peaks at 08:00 and 19:00, when demand peaks, and is lowest
at 03:00 and 14:00.

# Daily moves, power against the S&P 500

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_dm = POWER.groupby("date")["price"].mean()
_dm.index = pd.to_datetime(_dm.index)
_full = _dm.reindex(pd.date_range(_dm.index.min(), _dm.index.max(), freq="D"))
_ch = (_full.pct_change(fill_method=None) * 100).loc["2024"]
_prices = pd.read_csv("../data/prices.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
_spy = _prices[_prices["ticker"] == "SPY"].set_index("date")["close"].pct_change().loc["2024"] * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.6, 3.7))
ax.plot(_ch.index, _ch.clip(-100, 200), color=BLUE, linewidth=1.1)
ax.plot(_spy.index, _spy, color=AMBER, linewidth=2.2)
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=1)
ax.set_ylim(-110, 212)
ax.set_yticks([-100, -50, 0, 50, 100, 150, 200])
ax.set_yticklabels(["-100", "-50", "0", "50", "100", "150", "200+"])
ax.set_ylabel("change on the day before, %")
ax.annotate("West Denmark,\nthe day's average price", xy=(1.01, 110), xycoords=("axes fraction", "data"),
            color=BLUE, fontsize=11.5, fontweight="bold", va="center")
ax.annotate("S&P 500", xy=(1.01, 0), xycoords=("axes fraction", "data"), color=AMBER, fontsize=11.5,
            fontweight="bold", va="center")
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.dates.DateFormatter("%b"))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.08, right=0.8, top=0.96, bottom=0.1)
plt.show()
```

The day's average price moved more than 20 percent from the day before on 204
days of 2024. The S&P 500's largest daily move that year was 3.0 percent.


# Your turn [1]{.chip .chip-turn} {.your-turn}

Fill a dictionary with the median price at 03:00, 08:00, 13:00 and 18:00, then
get all 24 medians in one line with `groupby`.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
medians = {}
for h in [3, 8, 13, 18]:
    medians[h] = ...
    print(h, medians[h])

print(power.groupby(...)[...].median())
```


# Your turn 1: answer

```python
medians = {}
for h in [3, 8, 13, 18]:
    medians[h] = power[power['hour'] == h]['price'].median()
    print(h, medians[h])

print(power.groupby('hour')['price'].median())
```

```
3 626.47
8 844.57
13 550.56
18 895.19
```

The mask inside the loop keeps one hour at a time, and `groupby` does all 24 at
once. The median at 18:00 is 43 percent above the median at 03:00.

Within each hour, `shift(1)` moves the prices down one row, so each row gets
the day before's price. Returns within each ticker were built the same way.


# The label

```{pyodide}
power['price_before'] = power.groupby('hour')['price'].shift(1)
power['up'] = (power['price'] > power['price_before']).astype(int)

print(power.loc['2023-11-14 13:00':'2023-11-14 16:00', ['price_before', 'price', 'up']])
```

An hour's label `up` is 1 when it costs more than the same hour the day before.
The first day of the table has no day before, so its `price_before` is empty.


# The wind change

```{pyodide}
power['wind_change'] = power['wind'] - power.groupby('hour')['wind'].shift(1)

change_bands = pd.cut(power['wind_change'], [-np.inf, -1000, -300, 300, 1000, np.inf])
print(power.groupby(change_bands)['up'].mean())
```

`wind_change` is tomorrow's wind forecast minus today's. When it falls by more
than 1,000 MW, 86 percent of hours rise; when it rises that much, 12 percent.


The dots are the share of hours that rose, and the red curve is a logistic
regression on the wind change. Drag the slider to read its probability.


# The weekday, as one number or seven columns [play]{.chip .chip-predict}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(W.emit(W.weekday(DATA)))
```

As one number, the weekday can only tilt the week one way. As seven columns,
each day gets its own level, and the dots sit on the bars.


# Weekday columns in code

```{pyodide}
dummies = pd.get_dummies(power['weekday'], prefix='weekday', dtype=int)
days = []
for c in dummies:
    power[c] = dummies[c]
    days.append(c)
print(days)
```

`get_dummies` turns the weekday into seven columns of zeros and ones, and the
loop copies each into the table and keeps its name. On every row exactly one of
them is 1.


# Today's move

```{pyodide}
power['change_before'] = power['price_before'] - power.groupby('hour')['price'].shift(2)

move_bands = pd.cut(power['change_before'], [-np.inf, -200, -50, 50, 200, np.inf])
print(power.groupby(move_bands)['up'].mean())
```

`shift(2)` reaches two days back, so `change_before` is today's move. After a
fall of over 200 kroner, 60 percent of hours rise; after such a rise, 42.


# The rows to learn from

```{pyodide}
power = power.dropna()
train = power.loc[:'2023']
test = power.loc['2024']

print(len(train), len(test))
print(1 - test['up'].mean())
```

`dropna` removes the first two days, which have no day before. Calling no hour
of 2024 up, the majority rule, is right 50.3 percent of the time.


# A rule of thumb

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

rule = (test['wind_change'] < 0).astype(int)
print(accuracy_score(test['up'], rule))
```

The rule says up whenever tomorrow's wind forecast is lower than today's. It is
right 71.9 percent of the time in 2024, against 50.3 for the majority rule.


# Logistic regression on the wind change

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

model = Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('logit', LogisticRegression())])
model.fit(train[['wind_change']], train['up'])
p = model.predict_proba(test[['wind_change']])[:, 1]
print(roc_auc_score(test['up'], p))
```

With one column the model ranks the hours in the same order as the wind change
itself: an AUC of 0.796. What it adds is a probability for every hour.


# Adding columns one kind at a time

```{pyodide}
ladder = {'+ weekday as a number': ['wind_change', 'weekday'],
          '+ weekday as 7 columns': ['wind_change'] + days,
          "+ today's move": ['wind_change'] + days + ['change_before']}
for name in ladder:
    model.fit(train[ladder[name]], train['up'])
    p = model.predict_proba(test[ladder[name]])[:, 1]
    print(name, round(roc_auc_score(test['up'], p), 4))
features = ladder["+ today's move"]
```

Each step adds one kind of column, and the AUC rises from 0.796 to 0.833. After
the loop, `p` holds the probabilities of the last model, the one with all three.


# C on the folds

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, GridSearchCV

folds = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
grid = {'logit__C': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}
search = GridSearchCV(model, grid, cv=folds, scoring='roc_auc')
search.fit(train[features], train['up'])
print(search.best_params_, search.best_score_)
```

The folds move forward in time. Every C from 0.01 to 10 scores 0.815 on them,
so the penalty barely matters here.

A small C pulls every coefficient toward zero and the probabilities toward one

# The confusion matrix


At one half the model catches 3,171 of the 4,303 hours that rose, a recall of

For each hour of 2024, bet 1 MWh on the direction: long when the probability is
high, short when it is low. Each trade earns the move and pays a cost of 50 kroner.


# The move in each hour

```{pyodide}
move = test['price'] - test['price_before']

print(round(move.abs().sum()))
print(round(move.sum()))
```

Knowing every direction in advance, with no cost, would earn 1,868,568 kroner
in 2024. Always going long earns 514, because the rises and falls almost cancel.


# A function for the P&L

```{pyodide}
def pnl(p, move, threshold, cost):
    long = p >= threshold
    short = p <= 1 - threshold
    trades = long.sum() + short.sum()
    return round(move[long].sum() - move[short].sum() - cost * trades)

print(pnl(p, move, 0.5, 50))
print(pnl(p, move, 0.6, 50))
```

At one half every hour is traded, and the model earns 879,112 kroner after costs.
At 0.6 the hours near one half are left out, and it earns 957,809.

# What the P&L leaves out

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**The cost** <span>of 50 kroner per MWh is a round number for fees and the bid-ask spread, not a measured one.</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**The size** <span>of 1 MWh moves no price. A large bet placed in the auction would move the price against itself.</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**The contract** <span>that pays the change from one day to the next at one hour does not exist. The bet stands in for a buyer who can move use between days.</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**The forecast** <span>in the file comes out at 18:00, after the auction, so the model saw a slightly better forecast than a bidder has.</span>
:::
:::

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 5

A second label on the level of the price, an hour above 1,000 kroner, fitted

# Prices above 1,000 kroner

```{pyodide}
power['above_1000'] = (power['price'] > 1000).astype(int)

print(power['above_1000'].groupby(power.index.year).mean())
```

In 2022, 70 percent of the hours cost more than 1,000 kroner, and in 2024, 6
percent. The share that rose from the day before stayed near half in every year.


# Two training windows

```{pyodide}
levels = ['wind', 'solar'] + days
crisis = Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('logit', LogisticRegression())])
crisis.fit(power.loc[:'2023', levels], power.loc[:'2023', 'above_1000'])
calm = Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('logit', LogisticRegression())])
calm.fit(power.loc['2023', levels], power.loc['2023', 'above_1000'])

print(crisis.predict_proba(test[levels])[:, 1].mean())
print(calm.predict_proba(test[levels])[:, 1].mean())
```

With 2022 and 2023 the model expects 40 percent of 2024's hours above 1,000
kroner, and with 2023 alone 13; the share was 6.


# Predicted against actual [play]{.chip .chip-predict}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(W.emit(W.crisis(DATA)))
```

Each dot is a group of 2024's hours. With 2022 in training, a probability near
0.3 meant 0.8 percent; with 2023 alone, 15 percent.


# AUC against the Brier score

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss

happened = power.loc['2024', 'above_1000']
for m in [crisis, calm]:
    q = m.predict_proba(test[levels])[:, 1]
    print(roc_auc_score(happened, q), brier_score_loss(happened, q))
```

Both models rank 2024's hours equally well, with AUCs of 0.839 and 0.838. Only
the Brier score shows the difference: 0.187 against 0.062.


# Handling a changed market

# 6 · Similar hours {.divider}

Part 6

# Three classes

```{pyodide}
change = power['price'] - power['price_before']
power['move'] = pd.cut(change, [-np.inf, -50, 50, np.inf], labels=['lower', 'about the same', 'higher'])
three = Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('logit', LogisticRegression())])
three.fit(power.loc[:'2023', features], power.loc[:'2023', 'move'])
predicted_move = three.predict(test[features])
print(accuracy_score(power.loc['2024', 'move'], predicted_move))
```

`pd.cut` makes three classes: more than 50 kroner down, less than 50 either way,
and more than 50 up. The majority rule scores 0.381 and the model 0.606.


# The three-class confusion matrix

```{pyodide}
order = ['lower', 'about the same', 'higher']
actual = power.loc['2024', 'move']

print(confusion_matrix(actual, predicted_move, labels=order))
```

Rows are what happened, from lower to higher. The model never predicts about
the same: in no hour of 2024 is it the most likely of the three.


# A big move either way [play]{.chip .chip-predict}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(W.emit(W.vshape(DATA)))
```

A move of more than 150 kroner is most likely when the wind forecast changes a
lot, either way. A logistic regression on the wind change can only slope one way.


# The size of the wind change

```{pyodide}
power['big'] = (change.abs() > 150).astype(int)
power['size_wind_change'] = power['wind_change'].abs()

big_model = Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('logit', LogisticRegression())])
for cols in [features, features + ['size_wind_change']]:
    big_model.fit(power.loc[:'2023', cols], power.loc[:'2023', 'big'])
    q = big_model.predict_proba(power.loc['2024', cols])[:, 1]
    print(roc_auc_score(power.loc['2024', 'big'], q))
```

`abs` builds the size of the wind change, a shape a linear model cannot make
from the change itself. The AUC for a big move rises from 0.559 to 0.670.


# The k nearest hours [play]{.chip .chip-predict}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(W.emit(W.knn(DATA)))
```

k-NN finds the k hours of 2022 and 2023 most like this one and reports the share
that rose. Untick the scaler, and the weekday stops counting.


# k-NN in code

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

near = ['wind_change', 'change_before', 'weekday', 'hour']
knn = Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('knn', KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=201))])
knn.fit(train[near], train['up'])
print(roc_auc_score(test['up'], knn.predict_proba(test[near])[:, 1]))
```

k-NN needs no weekday columns: the nearest hours to a Monday are Mondays. With k
of 201, chosen on the folds, it scores 0.844 against the logistic regression's 0.833.


# k-NN without the scaler

```{pyodide}
bare = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=201)
bare.fit(train[near], train['up'])

print(roc_auc_score(test['up'], bare.predict_proba(test[near])[:, 1]))
print(train[near].std())
```

Without the scaler the AUC falls to 0.797, since the wind change spreads over
thousands of megawatts and the weekday over seven values.

# Everything used today {.smaller}

::: {.recap-grid}
::: {.recap-item}
**Looking at a market**
`read_csv` with `parse_dates`, `set_index`, `.loc` by date, `groupby` by year
and by hour, `pd.cut` into bands, a bar chart and two lines.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Loops, dictionaries, functions**
A dictionary of medians filled by a loop, a loop that adds the weekday columns,
a ladder of models in a dictionary, and `pnl` on two sets of rows.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**A label from the day before**
`shift(1)` inside `groupby('hour')` puts the same hour of the day before on
every row. About half the hours rose, in every year.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Columns built from others**
The wind change gave an AUC of 0.796, the weekday as seven columns 0.830, and
today's move 0.833.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**The threshold and the cost**
The best threshold rose with the cost. Chosen on 2022 and 2023, 0.55 earned
928,247 kroner in 2024 at 50 kroner a trade.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Training rows from another market**
Trained through 2022, the model expected 40 percent of 2024's hours above 1,000
kroner. The share was 6 percent.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**A shape a line cannot make**
The size of the wind change took a big move's AUC from 0.559 to 0.670, and k-NN
found the shape by itself.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**k-NN and the scoreboard**
The weekday and the hour as plain numbers, scaled: an AUC of 0.844. On your
eight hours k-NN scored 0.166 and logistic regression 0.194.
:::
:::
